<x_0.0635><y_0.9273>NANKING, a city of China, and capital of the pro<x_0.4473><y_0.9484><class_Text>

<x_0.4736><y_0.0625>vince of Kiang-nan, is said to have been formerly one of the most beautiful and flourishing cities in the world. When the Chinese speak of its extent, they say, if two borocons should go out by the same gate, and ride round it on full speed, taking different direc-tions, they would not meet before night. This account is evidently exaggerated, but it is certain, that Nan- surpasses in extent all the other cities of China. We are assured that its walls are five leagues and a half in circumference.<x_0.8691><y_0.2031><class_Text>

<x_0.4668><y_0.2023>This city is situated at the distance of a league from the river Kung-se-kking: it is of an irregular figure ; the mountains which are within its circumference having prevented its long ballot on a regular plan. It was forward to the imperial city; for this reason it was called _Nan-King_, which signifies, the Southern Court; yet but since the six grand tribunals have been transferred from hence to Peking; it is called _Kiang-ning_ in all the public acts.<x_0.8633><y_0.325><class_Text>

<x_0.4678><y_0.3234>Nan-king has lost much of the ancient splendor: is had formerly a magnificent place, no vestige of which is now to be seen, an observatory as present neglected, temples, tombs of the corpora, and other superb mo-uments, of which nothing remains but the remote brance. A third of the city is detected, but the rest is well inhabited. Some quarters of it are extremely po-phouse and full of business; particularly the mandorteur of a species of cotton cloth, of which great quantities we imported into Europe under the name of Nan- Kin. The streets are not so broad in these of Peking they are; however, very beautiful, well paved, and bonded with rich shops?<x_0.8584><y_0.5016><class_Text>

<x_0.4688><y_0.5>In this case resides one of those great mandarines called _Tsong-gion_, who takes cognizance of all import-ants affairs, not only of both the governments of the province, but also of those of the province of Kiang-si. The Tartars have a numerous garrison here, command-el by a general of their own nation ; and they occupy a quarter of the city, separated from the next by a plain wall.<x_0.8564><y_0.6102><class_Text>

<x_0.4697><y_0.6094>The palaces of the manharies, whether Chinese or Taxters, are in this city neither larger nor better birth than those in the capital cities of other provinces. Here are no public officers corresponding to the reputation of so celebrated a city, except by its gates, which are very beautiful; and some temples, among which is the fronome portadent tower. It is 200 feet high, and dividled into nine states by plain boards within, and without by comicses and small projections covered with green treinished tiles. There's an ascent of 40 steps to the first story; between each of the others there are 21.<x_0.8477><y_0.7719><class_Text>
